title: Atomic variable (CAS)
points: An atomic variable (AtomicInteger, AtomicLong) updates a single value without a lock by using a hardware compare-and-set (CAS) instruction.
CAS means: set the value to new only if it is still the expected old value; if another thread changed it, the CAS fails and the code retries.
It is lock-free, so there is no blocking or deadlock, but it only protects one variable.
It cannot protect an invariant across several variables, such as checking and booking a seat.
trade: Use for counters, flags and sequence ids. Versus locks: faster under low-to-moderate contention, no deadlock, but single variable only. Under heavy contention retries spin and waste CPU. For multi-variable invariants use a lock.
test: Why can an AtomicBoolean not safely solve the seat-booking problem when a booking updates the seat owner and the available-seat count?
answer: Atomics make one variable atomic. Booking changes two pieces of state that must stay consistent, so you need a lock around both.

questions.question: What does compareAndSet(expected, new) do?
options: Locks the variable and sets it
Sets the value only if it still equals expected, otherwise fails so the caller can retry
Always sets the value and returns the old one
Waits until the value equals expected
questions.explanation: CAS is a single hardware step: compare and swap if unchanged. It does not block; the caller retries on failure.

questions.question: Which is the right tool for a request counter shared by many threads?
questions.explanation: A single variable is the textbook atomic case. A lock works but costs more.

questions.question: Why are atomics a poor fit for 'if seat free then mark taken and decrement available'?
options: They protect only one variable, not an invariant over several
questions.explanation: Each atomic is safe on its own, but another thread can interleave between the two updates.
